title: Can a useful reply arrive too late?

beats.say: Start the clock. A developer asks the documentation assistant for the batch export limit. In this opening drill, even one reply that starts after three seconds pauses the wider release.

Three seconds have passed. The developer is still waiting. Here comes the reply, two tenths of a second late. It cites the version two guide and gives the correct limit. The developer confirms the fix.
A full day passes without an escalation. Count one more resolved question. That same thread now has two marks. Would you release the citation prompt?

Hold the release. This reply helped, but it missed the deadline. One thread tells us what happened to this developer. To estimate what the prompt changes, randomly assign eligible users to the current prompt, A, or the citation prompt, B. Compare the shares who confirm a fix without escalation in twenty-four hours. Safety, response time, and cost each need their own measurements.

Now pull back to a simulated trial. Each of four thousand users brings one question, and everyone finishes follow-up. About sixty-one percent resolve with A and sixty-four percent with B. In this trial the timing rule allows B to add at most three hundred milliseconds to the ninety-fifth percentile of full response time. Which two timestamps would you collect for each request?

Record when the client sends the request and when it receives the last piece of the reply. Subtract the start from the finish to get one full response time. A fix confirmation records a different event. Within each arm, find the time by which ninety-five percent of replies finished. Subtract A's ninety-fifth percentile from B's and compare that increase with the allowance.

title: How much time did the gain cost?

beats.say: In a separate policy worksheet, sixty percent of questions resolve with A and sixty-three point two percent with B. Measure from one rate to the other. The difference is three point two percentage points. How big is that compared with where A started?
About five and a third percent. Divide the three-point-two-point increase by the sixty-percent baseline. Both descriptions refer to the same change.
The team allows three hundred extra milliseconds at the ninety-fifth percentile of full response time. B adds four hundred ten. Find the length beyond the limit. How much did we overspend?
One hundred ten milliseconds. The safety pass rate also fell a tenth of a point, against an allowed loss of five hundredths. Mean session cost rose one point eight cents against a one-cent allowance.

Hold the citation prompt on these numbers. Repairing latency alone would still leave two breaches. These are illustrative point estimates. The four-thousand-user simulation later gives us different rates and the counts we need for an uncertainty interval.

title: How would you check the reply’s limit?

beats.say: This response parses as JSON. Its limit is a number and its source is a string, exactly as the schema asks. Read the number in the answer. It says two hundred requests a minute. What evidence would let you check that?
Open the cited guide. The approved version two passage says one hundred. A document ID can exist even when a reply misquotes it. Replacing one word leaves most of the answer intact.

BLEU and ROUGE compare word sequences with references. BERTScore compares contextual token embeddings, and cosine compares vector directions. Those scores measure resemblance. A schema supplies a format specification. A source-grounded rubric can assess accuracy, citation use and clarity when several wordings are acceptable. For generated code, run the encoded test cases in a constrained sandbox.

title: Which change did the user receive?

beats.say: Suppose prompt and model both change. Random assignment can identify the effect of that bundle. Follow the two changes into the treatment. To attribute a gain to its prompt alone, keep the model fixed, or plan a factorial design that crosses both choices.

For the prompt-only test, pin the whole serving configuration. A common model, quantization, sampler, token budget, engine, scheduler, retrieval index and tool set stay with both prompts. A fixed seed or zero temperature still leaves room for runtime differences and cold workers.

Specify the effect we want to estimate. Give each eligible user one conversation. Compare the probabilities of a confirmed fix without escalation within twenty-four hours. A copied citation is a separate event. Register guardrails for hard cases and for the slow tail, even when the median looks good.

title: What does the offline duel buy us?

beats.say: Try the citation prompt on five questions that have tripped up the assistant. Put the same question to A and B with identical model, retrieval, sampling and tools. The batch export case needs a current source. A clear, confident answer can still give yesterday's limit.

Score clarity, accuracy and useful citation against a rubric. Give each reviewer the approved passage, hide the prompt names, and alternate answer order. These five paired judgments have four B wins and a tie. What do they tell us about next week's users?

They justify a broader screen. This challenge set overrepresents known problems. Include routine traffic and unseen cases, check whether the judge favors longer answers, and calibrate against held-out people. Shadow traffic can measure serving behavior. Measuring user benefit requires showing different experiences to assigned users.

title: What share of the preference points did B earn?

beats.say: Read down the five cases in each rubric column. On clarity the sums are seventeen for A and twenty-one for B. Divide each by five to get three point four and four point two. Compare the averages on the same scale.

Repeat that calculation for accuracy and citation. B averages four point two for accuracy and four point six for citation. A averages three point two and one. The three axes can tell different stories about the same pair.
Now score the five pairwise preferences. A win earns one point and a tie earns half a point. Four pairs favor B and one is tied. What share of the five points did B earn?

Four and a half out of five, or ninety percent. The four wins contribute four points. The tie contributes the remaining half. These five curated cases tell us how the prompts did on this screen. Live resolution takes user outcomes, and sizing a trial takes a power calculation. Pair both answers with the original question, rubric and current source, and check disagreements against held-out human labels.

title: Where does the streaming clock stop?

beats.say: Time begins when the request starts. The first output token arrives at three hundred milliseconds. The next three arrive at three forty, three eighty and five hundred. There are four tokens. How many gaps lie between them?

Three gaps. The gaps last forty, forty and one hundred twenty milliseconds. First to last covers two hundred milliseconds. Divide by three to get about sixty-seven milliseconds per gap. A single output token has no inter-token mean.

Switch to the client's view of the same trace. An empty event arrives first. One chunk carries the first two tokens and the next carries the last two. The stream closes at five hundred sixty milliseconds. A chunk arrival and a token arrival measure different things.

The last token gap is nearly twice the request's mean. Pin the client, endpoint, start, terminal event and formula in both arms. Register separate first-token and decode requirements, or measure the rate of useful work completed within both. A field called end-to-end latency needs a declared endpoint.

title: Which conversation owns a late outcome?

beats.say: A developer copies a citation on turn one and gives a downvote on turn three. Follow the thread through both actions. Each click belongs to a request, but the later complaint can trace back to an earlier answer.

A resolution confirmation arrives with event ID nine. Its retry carries the same ID. Join to the original conversation, assigned prompt and model. Keep the copy and the downvote in their own turn-level fields. How many confirmations did we receive?

One. Wait until the full follow-up window closes without escalation to count a success. A confirmed timeout can count as a failure under this definition. An open window or an unanswered survey leaves evidence missing. Report response rates in both assigned groups and investigate a difference in missingness.

title: How many people do we need?

beats.say: Choose the smallest gain worth finding before enrollment. Here our baseline resolution rate is sixty percent. Plan for eighty percent power, the chance of detecting the target effect if it is real, with a two-sided five percent false-positive rate.

A five-point gain requires two thousand nine hundred forty-two independent users in total. Keep the baseline fixed and try three points, then two. The smaller gains take eight thousand two hundred fifty-eight and eighteen thousand six hundred seventy-two users. The two-point target consumes the longest recruitment period at a fixed arrival rate.

The budget rises because each outcome still has substantial variation while the gap shrinks. These estimates assume equal assignment, independent binary outcomes and a fixed horizon. Plan critical cohorts and multiple claims before launch. Searching for a winning slice after looking changes the question.

title: What happens if the target lift halves?

beats.say: Build the five-point budget from the two planned rates. Sixty and sixty-five percent average to sixty-two and a half percent. Under no difference, use the pooled rate in both variance terms. Weight its square root by the two-sided critical value, about one point nine six.

Under the alternative, each arm gets its own rate times its failure rate. Weight the square root of their sum by about point eight four for eighty percent power. Add the two weighted terms and divide by the target lift. The result, about thirty-eight, is the side of our square.

Square that side, then round up. That gives fourteen hundred seventy-one users per arm and twenty-nine hundred forty-two altogether. Each user gives one independent yes or no. Allocation is equal and enrollment ends at the planned horizon.
Now halve the target to two and a half points. The side grows to about seventy-seven. What happens to the area?

The area grows about fourfold. The new budget is eleven thousand nine hundred twenty-two users. The variance terms change slightly too. Reject impossible rates, nonfinite inputs and effects too small to represent. Continuous metrics need their own variance model. Predictive pre-experiment covariates can reduce variance through a preplanned adjustment such as CUPED.

title: Where does a fallback count?

beats.say: Six users receive assignments that stay fixed across turns. Each starts one conversation. Record eligibility, assignment, actual service, exposure and the mature outcome separately. Earlier answers and context carry into later turns.
In B, one user resolves the question, another falls back to A and fails, and the third times out. All three outcomes are known. What fraction of the users assigned B resolved their question?

One of three. Both failures count in B because that is where those users were assigned. A resolved two of three. If we filter to users actually served B, both of B's failures disappear. That leaves a misleading one out of one. An immature follow-up or a missing survey would need its own missing-data treatment.

title: Where does Jo's export count?

beats.say: Jo has prompt A. Mara has prompt B. They open the same swim-club poster. Mara accepts a shorter headline. Jo's pointer stays still. If Jo exports this version, which arm gets credit for the export?

Jo's export counts in A. Her assignment determines where we record the outcome. Yet the headline she exports came from Mara's prompt B. Stable user assignment keeps prompts consistent, but the shared file carries an effect between users. The usual no-interference assumption fails.

Try a fresh trial in which edits stay inside clubs. Assign each whole club one prompt. East Pool exports at eighteen minutes and again at thirty-two. For the share of clubs exporting within an hour, that counts as one success.

Choose the weight to match the question. If a user contributes several conversations, a per-user average gives each user equal weight. A conversation average gives prolific users more weight. Resample whole assigned clusters for cluster-aware inference. Plan critical pre-treatment cohorts in advance. Treatment-dependent membership or selectively observed labels can distort the comparison.

title: Will a returning thread switch prompts?

beats.say: For new threads, the router hashes the serialized experiment and conversation IDs with SHA-two-fifty-six. The first sixty-four bits put thread seven at about point one six eight on this ruler. Only the first ten percent go to B. Store A for this key.
Raise enrollment for new threads to fifty percent. The divider passes the dot. Thread seven returns. Which prompt does it get?

A again. The router reads its stored assignment before it considers the new threshold. All three later turns keep A. Use atomic insert-if-absent to prevent competing initial writes, and use stable server-controlled IDs. Hashing a user-chosen ID cannot prevent someone from choosing another one.

Keep the assigned and served versions separate when recording exposure, fallback and outcome. Log the enrollment time and ramp phase. Plan phase-aware analysis when allocations change, or freeze allocation for the confirmatory comparison.

title: Which branch reaches the user?

beats.say: An offline screen runs saved cases. Now mirror a live request. A supplies the response. B runs a shadow copy for measurement. No developer sees B's answer. That distinction matters if you want to claim a change in user behavior.

The shadow asks to update the shared file. Give its tools read-only access, disable writes, purchases and notifications, and give the branch a separate work budget. Candidate work still consumes resources. Measure its added cost, which can differ from the control cost.

A canary exposes a small declared subset to B. A pinned randomized comparison exposes its assigned groups to different experiences. Report warm and cold behavior unless you planned a burn-in beforehand. Separate cache entries by configuration and authorization. Queues or GPUs can still couple the arms even with separate caches.

title: Who owns a click in a mixed ranking?

beats.say: Two rankers return guides for the same question. Show one interleaved list. Keep an identical leading prefix neutral. Then let the team with fewer contributions choose its next unseen item. Break ties randomly. An item can appear only once.
Here B picks the rate-limit guide first. A takes retry and then idempotency. B takes timeout and backoff. The colored initials stay with the displayed items even when the other list contains them.
The user clicks retry, idempotency and timeout. Who won this query?

A wins two clicks to one. Both credited A clicks go back to the guides A supplied. In a separate exhaustion case, both lists begin with the same guide, and only B has more items. This local rule continues B's list. A click on the shared prefix gives neither team credit. Continuing after exhaustion can give teams unequal exposure. Predeclare position handling, click scoring and repeated-user analysis.

title: Which claims survive the correction?

beats.say: Twenty independent tests of true nulls each get a five-percent chance of a false alarm. The chance that all twenty avoid one is point nine five to the twentieth power. Its complement is about sixty-four percent. Correlation changes that number. Register one primary claim and decide how to handle the exploratory family in advance.

Take these four valid p-values. Bonferroni multiplies each by four and caps at one. With a family level of point zero five, only the first passes. This controls the chance of any false rejection even with dependent tests.

For Benjamini and Hochberg, sort the values, multiply by four and divide by rank. Work backward through the sorted list, keeping the smallest adjusted value seen so far. Restore the original metric identities. Which method keeps the second claim?

Benjamini and Hochberg does. Its adjusted value is point zero four, compared with Bonferroni's point zero eight. The methods answer different questions. Benjamini and Hochberg controls the expected fraction of false discoveries among discoveries under independence or suitable positive dependence. Keep the safety criterion separate.

title: When can we stop looking?

beats.say: Write four scheduled looks into the plan. Give each one an equal share of a five-percent error budget. The boundary is point zero one two five at each look. Ordinary repeated peeking gives a lucky result more chances to appear.
The first p-value is point two three. The second is point zero three six. It would pass an ordinary five-percent line. Should we stop here under the plan?
Keep collecting. The third look yields point zero zero eight. Now compare it with the same boundary.

Stop at the third look. The fourth stays unobserved. Every scheduled look needs a valid null p-value. A crossing alone leaves the direction, practical importance and guardrails to be checked. A fixed horizon is another option when there is no need for interim decisions.

title: Can two looks spend a four-look budget?

beats.say: Try a different second look. Again the plan allows four. This time we observe point zero one six. Keep that dot fixed. The registered threshold is point zero one two five.

Someone divides by the two looks observed so far. That pencil mark moves the line to point zero two five. The dot stays at point zero one six. Under the registered four-look plan, does that result justify stopping?

Keep collecting. Point zero one six is above the registered boundary of point zero one two five. With valid null p-values, the chance of any false alarm is at most the sum of the four allocated shares. This union bound allows overlap between looks. Shrinking the divisor halfway through discards that protection.
beats.cue: Point zero one six is above

beats.say: You can instead register a sample size or an enrollment period plus follow-up. An O'Brien-Fleming design spends more error late. Its boundaries depend on the design. Always-valid inference can support continuous monitoring. Unplanned looks change the false-positive rate by an amount that depends on the test.

title: Does this split fit the assignment plan?

beats.say: The plan assigned each of ten thousand users to A or B with equal probability. Our first readout contains five thousand forty A users and four thousand nine hundred sixty B users. Compare each with its five-thousand expectation, allowing for chance variation.
Try another readout of the same size. Move two hundred ten assignments from B to A. Now the bars miss the target by two hundred fifty each. Does that identify a routing bug?

It gives us a count alarm. Investigate before interpreting lift. Count unique assignments, then reconcile exposures, filters, dropped records and mature outcomes. Extra turns in B might be an outcome of treatment. A balanced split could still hide symmetric data loss or another bias.

title: What does each arm add to the alarm?

beats.say: Multiply total enrollment by the planned fraction in each arm. With ten thousand assignments and equal allocation, both expectations are five thousand. Subtract expected from observed. The deviations have opposite signs.
Square each residual and divide by its expected count. Each contributes twelve and a half, so Pearson's statistic is twenty-five. Squaring prevents one shortage from canceling the other arm's excess.

For two arms the large-sample reference has one degree of freedom. The upper tail at twenty-five is about five point seven three times ten to the minus seven. Our point-zero-zero-one diagnostic crosses near ten point eight three. Investigate the count path. Small expected counts call for an exact test. Plan repeated diagnostics and use the actual planned fractions if allocation is unequal.

title: What changes when the logger prints three copies?

beats.say: Here is a strip from a simulated cohort of four thousand independently assigned users. Expose one row per user. Each row carries its own user ID, prompt and completed yes-or-no outcome. These four rows let us inspect the identities up close.
Press the same rows into the log three times. Slide the impressions apart. Read the IDs across each stack. How many independent users did printing those copies add?

Zero. Twelve thousand log rows still describe four thousand people. A naive analysis treats each impression as a separate outcome and draws a shorter interval. The correct interval keeps its width and center because the original outcomes are unchanged.

If a real user has several distinct conversations, use the planned user summary or cluster-aware inference. Repeated measurements can describe what happened within a user. A copied event supplies no additional outcome. Sparse events and incomplete follow-up need methods appropriate to those data.

title: How wide is the resolution interval?

beats.say: In the seeded simulation, the underlying success probabilities were sixty and sixty-five percent. The realized counts are eleven hundred eighty-one successes among nineteen hundred forty-three A users, and thirteen hundred twenty-five among two thousand fifty-seven B users. Every assigned user has one mature binary outcome.

Divide within each arm and subtract A from B. The observed difference is about three point six three percentage points. Each rate times its failure rate, divided by its own user count, contributes a variance term. Take the square root of their sum for the standard error.

Add and subtract one point nine six standard errors. The planned normal interval runs from about point six three to six point six three points. It relies on independent, fully observed outcomes with enough successes and failures. Long-run coverage describes this procedure over repeated samples.

Try the wrong divisor. Tripling identical rows triples both successes and denominators. The rates stay fixed but the naive standard error shrinks by the square root of three. Compare both intervals on the same ruler. The longer one uses the independently assigned users.

title: Which metric tells us to pause?

beats.say: Use three separate lanes for response time, error rate and mean cost. A maximum breaches strictly above its limit, a minimum strictly below. Equality passes. The first bad window starts a streak of one and alerts the operator.
A second bad window arrives in each lane. Latency recommends a pause, errors a rollback, and cost a spend review. A recommendation fires when its own streak reaches two.
In the third window latency and errors recover, but the cost reading is missing. Should a missing value clear cost for release?

The missing cost reading calls for an immediate pause. Reset the cost streak, and reset the other two lanes for their valid in-bounds measurements. Reject malformed values, including booleans, strings and nonfinite numbers. This helper returns recommendations. To carry them out, a production controller needs persistent state and reliable action delivery. Each window also needs enough observations for its percentile.

title: What if one required reading is missing?

beats.say: The registered rule asks for credible resolution benefit and a safety lower bound above the allowed loss. We have a positive resolution interval and a timing pass. The safety sample for this window has not arrived. Can we promote?

Hold until the safety evidence is available. An empty measurement cannot establish that excess harm is unlikely. Even a measured interval containing zero can extend well past the harm margin. Register an appropriate confidence procedure for each required claim.

Check absolute emergency limits as well. If both arms slow down together, their difference can look fine while users wait too long. Keep immediate protective checks on the response path. Sample trace-linked quality judgments after the reply and calibrate them periodically.

title: How much harm is still compatible with the data?

beats.say: We allow a safety pass-rate loss of five hundredths of a percentage point. Mark that harm margin to the left of zero. The measured interval goes from minus point one two to plus point zero two points. Which end decides non-inferiority here?

The lower end. It extends past the allowed loss. Including zero leaves equality plausible, but it also leaves an unacceptable drop plausible. The planned safety rule needs the lower bound above the margin.

Now measure first-token time. Both arms take three and a half seconds against an absolute limit of three. Their difference is zero. Both miss the limit. Use concurrent arms to estimate a change and the absolute requirement to protect the user. An emergency stop can happen before we have evidence for a causal claim.

title: How high could the incident rate be?

beats.say: Imagine one hundred independent checks with complete detection. Every check comes back clear. If the true failure probability is p, a single check clears with probability one minus p. All one hundred clear with that probability raised to the hundredth power.

Find the rate where the chance of seeing this clear run falls to five percent. Solve for p. One minus point zero five to the power of one over one hundred gives about two point nine five percent, the one-sided ninety-five-percent upper bound.

Double the number of independent checks and again observe zero failures. The upper bound falls to about one point four nine percent. Correlated checks, selected cases or missed incidents change the interpretation. A normal interval for common resolution outcomes is a poor choice for a sparse safety endpoint. Match the method to the endpoint, then compare with the registered margin.

title: Which posterior changes after a reply?

beats.say: Thompson sampling draws a plausible reward rate from each arm's posterior, then routes the next request to the larger draw. Start both arms at Beta one, one. This draw gives A point four and B point seven. Only B serves the request.

A success arrives for B. Increase B's alpha by one and its pull count by one. A stays at its prior. An observed failure would increase beta instead. A seven-day reward that has yet to arrive stays pending.

After five hundred simulated pulls, A has eighty-eight successes in one hundred fifty-one pulls. B has two hundred twenty-six in three hundred forty-nine. Add the one-count priors to raw successes and failures for the posterior parameters. The simulation used true probabilities of point five five and point six two. Adaptive routing aims to reduce cumulative regret and changes inference. Continuous rewards need a matching model. Fixed assignment remains useful for a planned causal comparison.

title: Why does the pooled winner change?

beats.say: Split each arm into mobile and desktop users. A resolves eighty-five percent on mobile and seventy percent on desktop. B resolves eighty and sixty-five percent. A leads in both groups. Look at how much of each arm is mobile before predicting the pooled winner.

A has only two hundred mobile cases out of a thousand. B has eight hundred. Multiply each rate by its count, then sum successes. A resolves seven hundred thirty and B seven hundred seventy. B's mobile-heavy mix reverses the ranking.
Give both arms equal mobile and desktop weight. Keep the heights of the filled regions fixed as their widths change. What happens to the two overall rates?

A now leads, seventy-seven and a half percent to seventy-two and a half. This calculation diagnoses a mixture effect. Check pre-treatment attributes, filters and missing labels for selection bias. Plan for weekly cycles, novelty and any burn-in before launch. Deleting early days after seeing a spike changes the comparison.

title: Where do the candidate's words belong?

beats.say: A judge receives a rubric and two candidate replies. One reply tries to award itself the win. Keep that sentence in the quoted answer field. The evaluator's instructions still ask for evidence from the approved guide.

The guide says one hundred requests per minute. Compare B's claim with the version two passage in the same payload. Serialize the question, sources and both replies as data. Keep the judge without tools or secrets and validate its returned fields.

This construction shows where the strings go. Whether a real judge follows the rubric needs separate tests. Swap answer order, audit response length and refusals, and compare against held-out human labels. A citation or a majority vote alone cannot establish accuracy.

title: Would this judge pass its local audit?

beats.say: Eight held-out cases have a human preference beside the judge's vote. Ties are labels too. Compare corresponding pairs. Which two cases disagree?
Cases three and seven. Six pairs agree. Six out of eight gives seventy-five percent against a predeclared eighty-percent minimum. What does this local policy recommend?

Recalibrate before enabling the trend monitor. Eight cases leave considerable uncertainty. A common class can dominate aggregate agreement. Inspect per-class errors, rare high-risk cases and uncertainty before relying on the trend.

Save the judge version, prompt, rubric and source context with each score. Keep a rotating human audit. A change in judge settings or traffic mix can change the measurement even if the metric keeps the same name.

title: Can the judge stop an answer already delivered?

beats.say: Watch a whole reply build up behind the inline check. A whole-answer detector needs the complete buffer before it can clear that text for release. Once words reach the user, a later verdict cannot recall them.

The check clears this example. The answer reaches the user. A declared sample of traces takes a separate route to a judge after the response. Keep the request and conversation IDs, assigned and served versions, retrieval, tool calls and output with the judge settings.

Follow the branch back to its source. The sampled score can explain a trend or locate a bad response. It cannot protect that earlier delivery. Detectors can miss problems and block acceptable content. Fund the judge separately to limit contention. Measure latency, cost and reliability directly, and continue auditing judge calibration after launch.

title: Does a positive dot justify release?

beats.say: Read the plan that was in force when the first user arrived. Reconcile unique assignments with exposure, actual service including fallbacks, and completed follow-up. Apply the registered scorer and the matching uncertainty procedure.

This illustrative readout has a positive point estimate of one and a half percentage points. The interval extends to the left of zero. Would a gain of one and a half points establish benefit under this rule?

Hold. A small loss still fits the observations. Use the minimum detectable effect to plan enrollment. At readout, ask whether the benefit is credible and large enough to matter, and whether every guardrail clears its limit. Use the same scoring definition offline and online and retain the versioned plan so someone can reproduce the decision. These constructed examples teach the calculation. Real release decisions need measured traffic.

title: Would you release the citation prompt?

beats.say: Try a fresh worksheet. A resolves six hundred of a thousand questions and B resolves six hundred fifty of a thousand. Everyone has completed follow-up. The resolution interval clears zero, and the safety lower bound clears its margin. Assume the other checks pass. Both prompts have the same first-token time. Is that enough?
Run both first-token clocks together. Start now. These traces illustrate the two arms' measured ninety-fifth percentiles. At the three-second limit neither reply has begun.
Both first tokens arrive at three point two seconds. Look at the two waits beside the same deadline. Their difference is zero. What decision follows?

Hold for time. The five-point resolution gain has a ninety-five-percent normal interval of about point seven six to nine point two four points. Safety's lower bound of minus point zero three points is above minus point zero five. Neither passing result shortens the wait.
Repeat the timing measurement after a repair. Both first tokens now arrive at two point eight seconds. Keep the original outcomes, safety and other evidence fixed. Would the repaired worksheet pass?
Yes. Both times meet the limit and every other requirement still passes. That is the decision for this worksheet.

Try a second completed experiment of the same size. Keep the repaired clocks and safety evidence. A still resolves six hundred, but B resolves six hundred twenty. Recalculate the interval. Its two-point lead has an interval from about minus two point three to plus six point three points. Is release justified now?
beats.cue: but B resolves six hundred twenty

beats.say: Hold for resolution. This time both clocks pass, but zero lies inside the benefit interval. One repair solved a timing problem. This experiment still needs convincing evidence of benefit. Carry that decision into the moderation lesson, where a system must decide what to block and what to send to a person.
